cells.tense: The fire is yours right now and you're tending it, hand on the work, awake to what you're building today
cells.ask: Pick the next step that comes from something you actually want and say it out loud at the table before you move. It hands the motive back to you.
cells.core:
You start things and you stay with them. That steady warmth is running here — you keep your own direction lit without turning the keeping into a performance for anyone, and the people near you feel the difference even when they couldn't name it.

On an ordinary day it looks like noticing the shape a thing is taking and stepping toward it unhurried, without checking first whether it's allowed. There's room now for the next thing you imagine, not only the next thing you push through. Say the want plainly before you act on it and you'll find out whether the direction sharpens or softens — either way, you'll know it's yours.

cells.tense: You're gripping a future that's already crowded, willing the next move before it's yours to make
cells.ask: Name one thing you can set down for an hour and put it somewhere out of sight. It gives back the room to hear what you actually want next.
cells.core:
You're tending a fire for something that hasn't arrived. You know the step after this one and the one after that, and you're carrying the weight of making them all happen ahead of time, before anything has asked you to.

When it's working, direction comes from genuine engagement — you move because something is worth moving toward, not because you're bracing against a future you can't write in. On a good day that looks like doing the next thing in front of you and letting the one after that wait its turn. The grip isn't holding the momentum up; it's spending warmth you'd rather have later. Lift one thing off the pile right now and find out.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already behind you, still holding it open with both hands
cells.ask: Take one thing you're keeping alive that has clearly ended and say out loud to yourself that it's over — no fixing, just the sentence. It clears the way for something to move again.
cells.core:
You know how to keep a thing going long after it stopped giving anything back. That's a real skill, and it's the one currently handling your direction — nothing gets closed, so nothing new gets a clear road.

On an ordinary day it looks like letting a finished thing finish, and feeling relief rather than guilt when it does. There's nothing to repair in the saying; the sentence is the whole job. Pick one thing still held open and name it done, just to yourself. Direction tends to return after that gets said, not before.

cells.tense: You're already moving and you're doing it on purpose, but the way you describe it says it's happening to you
cells.ask: Pick one thing you did today that moved your own life forward and say the sentence 'I did that' out loud, to no one. It puts the doing back where it came from.
cells.core:
You're steering already. You choose what to keep going and what to let fade, and you do it with care — but you talk about the momentum as if it has a mind of its own, and the care gets filed under something other than you.

When it's working, the moving is yours the way your own handwriting is yours, and you can say so without ceremony. On a plain day that looks like doing the next right thing and knowing it was you who did it. Take one thing you did today that kept your direction alive and claim it out loud. Nobody needs the credit handed elsewhere, and the fire doesn't need the modesty.
cells.sheetLine: You're already at the wheel, and nobody else is driving.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say what keeps the person from starting, only that the capacity is under-expressed here; the cell must not invent a failure, a lesson, or a history behind it. A reader might reasonably say 'my problem isn't starting, it's that everything I start is taken from me' — so the asks stay a single visible act that doesn't require territory or permission. The asks survive being wrong: naming the want is useful even if wanting wasn't the actual issue, and dropping one load is worth doing even if it doesn't restore movement. The line that serves the writer more than the reader is any sentence that explains the mechanism of the seat or the map rather than saying what the person can see at their own table.
